name: SQL & Relational Databases
description: Designing relational schemas and querying, joining and aggregating data with SQL.

questions.question: Which clause filters individual rows before any grouping happens?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question: Which SQL statement changes values in existing rows?
questions.explanation: UPDATE modifies existing rows; ALTER changes table structure and INSERT adds new rows.

questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: Only rows that match in both tables
All rows from the right table only
Every combination of rows from both tables
All rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right, with NULLs where there is no match
questions.explanation: A LEFT (OUTER) JOIN keeps every left-table row; unmatched right-side columns are NULL.

questions.question: How does COUNT(column) differ from COUNT(*)?
options: COUNT(column) ignores rows where that column is NULL; COUNT(*) counts all rows
COUNT(*) ignores NULL rows; COUNT(column) counts all rows
questions.explanation: Aggregate functions on a column skip NULLs, while COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of content.

questions.question: What is a 'dirty read' in transaction isolation?
options: Reading data written by another transaction that has not yet committed
Reading the same row twice and getting different committed values
A new row appearing when a range query is repeated
questions.explanation: Dirty reads see uncommitted changes; the other options describe non-repeatable reads, phantom reads and corruption.

questions.question: A table is in 2NF, but a non-key column depends on another non-key column (a transitive dependency). Which normal form does it fail?
questions.explanation: 3NF requires that non-key attributes depend only on the key, with no transitive dependencies.

practical.title: Top customers by spend
practical.instructions: Tables: customers(id, name) and orders(id, customer_id, amount). Write one SQL query that returns each customer's name and total order amount, only for customers whose total exceeds 1000, sorted by total descending.
practical.expected_output: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 1000 ORDER BY total DESC;

rubric.hint: Use SUM(amount) to total each customer's orders.
Aggregates per customer require GROUP BY.
Filter aggregated totals with HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000, not WHERE.

tasks.title: Learn SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
tasks.description: Work through the first part of the PostgreSQL tutorial (creating tables, populating them, querying). Install PostgreSQL or use an online sandbox and run every example.
tasks.completion_criteria: You can create a table, insert rows and filter/sort them without notes.

tasks.title: Complete SQLBolt lessons 1-12
tasks.description: Complete the interactive SQLBolt lessons through joins and aggregates. Rewrite two of your answers in a different but equivalent way.
tasks.completion_criteria: Lessons 1-12 completed with all exercises solved.

tasks.title: Design and query a normalised schema
tasks.description: Design a schema for a small school (students, courses, enrolments) in 3NF with primary and foreign keys. Write 10 queries using joins, GROUP BY/HAVING and subqueries.
tasks.completion_criteria: Schema SQL file plus 10 working queries with expected results noted.

tasks.title: Build and tune a reporting database
tasks.description: Load a public dataset of at least 100k rows into PostgreSQL, write analytical queries with window functions, and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to add indexes that speed up the slowest query.
tasks.completion_criteria: Before/after EXPLAIN ANALYZE output showing a measurable speedup from an index.
